summary:
Pasco department has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern on record. It stands under the national framework of Peru, where trans identity is not criminalised, but where the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, repealed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and presided over rising recorded violence against trans women.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The text carries narrow exceptions for custody situations and where entry is otherwise required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The measure still required plenary backing at that point, and its reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

Trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho argues the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would fall to security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes, enacted in April 2025, whose Article 5.1 prohibits entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than a person's birth sex. The same legislative package bars inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute has documented trans people barred from public restrooms and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public life. SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where bathroom assignment was grounded on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Camacho stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three countries in the subregion, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The sources addressing the bathroom regime carry no Pasco-specific content; they describe the national legislative and judicial position against which this department is assessed. No departmental, provincial or municipal ordinance of Pasco is quoted, and no enforcement incident in Pasco is recorded in the inventory.

The legislative push has a documented national trigger rather than a local one: a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport. Enforcement logic cited by critics would place hotel, gym and transport security staff in the position of reading a DNI to determine whether a restroom user is trans.

Comparative placement is narrow. After the 2017 repeal, Peru stands with Paraguay and Guyana as the only three countries in the subregion whose hate-crime law omits LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, while the regional court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 points the opposite direction by framing gender identity as protected personal autonomy.

The Azul Rojas Marín judgment is of a kind not previously recorded in the region: it is described as the first torture-by-discrimination case decided by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, and it arrived through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights after years of litigation.

Recorded killings are widely understood to understate the position. The 2024 report's co-author states that the published figures are a sub-registry, so the 54 transgender and gender-diverse people killed between 2020 and 2023 represent documented cases only.
localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains a long, costly and invasive process for residents, which shapes what documents a trans person can present when a venue assigns restroom access by the sex recorded on the DNI.

Residents disputing restroom exclusion have a mixed record before the consumer-protection body: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's complaint against SmartFit after the company grounded bathroom assignment on the DNI, and a separate trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym enforcing the April 2025 policy was also dismissed.

Healthcare settings moved in a protective direction in June 2024, when national health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, a change described as a step toward dignity for trans patients.

Residents also retain a constitutional route: in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck down an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional, and IDEHPUCP grounds its challenge to Article 5 in Article 2(2) of the Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights.

Hate-crime protection is unavailable in domestic Penal Code terms for LGBT residents following the 2017 repeal, so protection in a bias-motivated attack must be sought outside those provisions; the Azul Rojas Marín case shows litigation can run for close to two decades before a conviction.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents any Pasco-specific trans ordinance, police practice, venue policy or complaint, so the department's own position is unresolved rather than assessed as permissive or restrictive.

Whether bills 6506 and 8457 were enacted separately from the April 2025 Law on the sexual integrity of children and adolescents is unresolved here; the inventory records the February 2025 committee approval and the separate April 2025 plenary approval of Article 5.1 without linking the two texts.

Whether venues in Pasco have altered restroom signage in response to the April 2025 provisions, and whether any departmental authority has issued guidance, is not sourced.

Local court or consumer-protection decisions arising inside Pasco on restroom or service exclusion are not sourced; the resolutions cited are national-level.

The claim that the article-4 content ban enables censorship of identity and artistic material rests on Human Rights Watch's assessment; no specific Pasco enforcement of that article is documented.
